method: Linear to linear: the polarization loss factor is cos^2(theta), where theta is the tilt between the two linear polarization axes in degrees, accepted from 0 to 90 inclusive (0 aligned, 90 orthogonal). The voltage coupling is cos(theta), the mismatch loss is -10 log10(PLF) dB, and the rejection applied to a signal polarized in the orthogonal plane is -10 log10(sin^2(theta)) dB. At 90 degrees no wanted signal couples, so the mismatch loss is reported as infinite; at 0 degrees the orthogonal rejection is infinite. Linear to circular: the axial ratio AR in dB, accepted from 0 to 40, gives the voltage ratio r = 10^(AR/20); the cross-polar discrimination is 20 log10((r+1)/(r-1)) dB and is infinite for a perfect 0 dB circular antenna; the loss to a linear antenna ranges from 10 log10(1 + 1/r^2) dB, when the linear axis is aligned with the major axis of the ellipse, to 10 log10(1 + r^2) dB, when it is aligned with the minor axis, and an ideal circular wave gives the fixed 3.01 dB at both ends. Coupling fractions below 1e-10 are treated as zero, so anything beyond 100 dB of rejection is reported as infinite. Voltage ratios are rounded half up to four decimals, power ratios to four decimals and decibel values to two. The tool models polarization match alone: it ignores ground reflection, multipath, Faraday rotation along the path, cross-polar pattern lobes, the orientation of the axial-ratio ellipse and antenna efficiency, and it is not a link-budget replacement. Everything is calculated in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: IEEE Std 145, IEEE Standard for Definitions of Terms for Antennas: polarization loss factor, axial ratio and cross-polar discrimination
Antenna measurement practice: cross-polar discrimination from axial ratio, XPD = 20 log10((r + 1) / (r - 1)) with r = 10^(AR/20)
Antenna theory: an ideal circularly polarized wave delivers half its power to a linearly polarized antenna, a fixed 3.01 dB
